query:
You are the rubber duck for an ASME Journal of Mechanical Design manuscript.
This is iteration 3 of 5, each with a different focus. Work by ADVERSARIAL
DIALOGUE and the SOCRATIC METHOD: write the session as an explicit
question-and-answer dialogue. For each probe, (a) pose the hardest question a
hostile expert referee would ask, (b) attempt to answer it yourself STRICTLY
from the attached materials (manuscript.pdf, supplementary.pdf, LaTeX sources,
references.bib, and the campaign data CSVs), quoting or citing the exact
passage or data you used, and (c) render a verdict: WITHSTANDS (the manuscript
answers it), WOUNDED (answerable but the text needs a specific change), or
FAILS (the manuscript cannot answer it and must change or soften). For every
WOUNDED or FAILS verdict, give the concrete edit you would make, at the level
of the sentence or number to change.

Context you should take as given rather than re-litigate: the campaign is
mid-flight. The nine-design Sobol seed round plus a reference prism are
printed; eight articles have completed 101-drop drop-tower sessions; a fully
Bayesian SAASBO surrogate was fit; nine round-2 designs are on the printer.
Round-2 results, the budget-matched baseline, the quasi-static Instron
campaign, and the metal-analog build are honestly declared placeholders; do
not flag their absence as a defect, but DO flag any place where the text
overclaims beyond the seed round. A prior adversarial review of the BO
objective stack (task 3e398131) already established: the rebound-energy
objective rests on an unvalidated ballistic interpretation, the
t180-versus-rebound trade-off is fragile at n=8, and per-drop SEM understates
article-level noise (about 0.72 percent CV); the manuscript now discloses all
three in its Discussion, so check the disclosure is faithful rather than
re-derive it.

The campaign data files attached are: t3-prism-bo-batch-drop-results.csv (one
row per tested article: stabilized objective means/sds over the 101-drop
session, ringdown descriptors, joined as-printed geometry and weighed mass),
t3-prism-bo-batch-print-key.csv (print IDs, masses, defects),
t3-prism-bo-suggestions-round1.csv (the model-recommended round-2 designs
with posterior predictions), and the round-1 Pareto figure PNG.

FOCUS OF THIS ITERATION: framing, novelty, and scope (title, abstract,
Sections 1, 2, and the novelty table). At minimum: (1) Attack the novelty
claim "no prior study closes a BO loop over co-printed multi-material
tensegrity-inspired hardware using physical impact measurements as the sole
ground truth" against the cited literature in references.bib (Pajunen 2019 and
2021, Bauer 2021, Intrigila 2022, Mo 2023, Santos 2023, Sabouni-Zawadzka
2024, Almeida 2025, Davami 2025, Wang 2026): is the claim stated with exactly
the right qualifiers, and does the novelty table's row for this work match
what was actually executed (SAASBO/qNEHVI on t180 and rebound energy, not SEA)?
(2) Is the planetary-lander motivation honest given the measured result that
most seed articles AMPLIFY peak shock, and does the testbed-not-flight-hardware
framing paragraph inoculate the paper adequately? (3) Does the abstract match
the body (objectives, budget, what is done versus planned), and is it within
JMD's length norms? (4) Is the tensegrity-inspired versus true-tensegrity
caveat (no pretension, extensible TPU) made early and consistently, and does
any sentence slip into claiming true tensegrity behavior? (5) Scope
discipline: does the out-of-scope list survive contact with what the
Discussion later claims?

info.name: run_cell
info.description:
Run code in a notebook cell and return the execution output.

This method allows running code in a new cell (append) or re-running
an existing cell with updated code.

Usage Examples:
    run_cell("print('Hello, world!')",
            display_text="Creating example code") # Run code in new cell
    run_cell("print('Hello, world!')",
            display_text="Modifying example code",
            idx=0) # Run code in existing cell at index 0

Error Recovery:
    When a cell fails with an error, you MUST fix it by calling run_cell
    with the corrected code and the SAME idx as the failed cell:

    run_cell("corrected_code", idx=3)  # Fix error in Cell #3

    The cell number is shown in the output prefix (e.g., "[Cell #3]").
    Do NOT create a new cell to fix an error - always edit the failed cell.

display_text.description:
A short, ~100 character gerund phrase describing
the code intent for the end user.
display_text.title: Display Text

idx.description:
Cell index to run. If None or >= len(cells), appends a new cell.
If provided, updates and re-runs the existing cell at that index.
Use this to fix errors in existing cells.
idx.title: Idx

info.name: reset_kernel

Reset the kernel to a clean state.

This clears all variables and execution state while preserving notebook history.

_unused.description:
Unused. Present so the tool schema has a property — OpenAI's

properties".
_unused.title: Unused

Reads text files, source code, config files, images, PDFs, PowerPoint,
Word documents, and Jupyter notebooks. For binary data files (Excel,

limit.description: Maximum number of lines/pages to read
limit.title: Limit

Start line (0-based) for text, or start page/slide (1-based) for PDFs/PowerPoint/
Word documents
offset.title: Offset

info.name: explore
info.description:
Search the workspace or memory for information.

Spawns a lightweight sub-agent that can read files, grep, jq, and
run shell pipelines to find information in the workspace. Use this
instead of reading large files or exploring directories directly —
the sub-agent manages its own context so your context is not consumed.

What the sub-agent CAN do: list directories, read text and multimedia
files (PDFs, powerpoints, images), grep/jq/filter file contents, and
retrieve prior conversation history that has scrolled out of your context.

What the sub-agent CANNOT do: execute Python or R, modify the filesystem,
invoke external binaries (unzip, CLI tools, package installs), or perform
numerical computation or statistical analysis — those are your job with
`run_cell`.

Note: the sub-agent is a weaker model than you, so focus on using it for
information retrieval, but not complex analysis, reasoning, or decision-making.
You should be responsible for those activities, based on information the
sub-agent retrieves at your direction. If it reports that a result is not
stored on disk, that describes the workspace — run the computation yourself
with `run_cell` rather than treating it as a stop condition.

Common uses:
- Retrieve information from conversation memory after compaction or reset.
- Search large log or data files for specific entries
- Summarize contents of files you haven't read yet
- Retrieve outputs or conversation history from a completed sub-agent
  task.

query.description:
What to find or summarize, e.g. "What datasets have I
downloaded so far?" or "Have I seen error X before, and how did I solve it?".
query.title: Query

info.name: view_docs
info.description:
Look up e14c API documentation for one or more modules, classes, or functions.

Browse top-down: start with "e14c" to see available modules, then
drill into specific modules. Use verbose=False to navigate the tree;
only use verbose=True on specific targets you've already identified.
Do not call view_docs speculatively at the start of a task — call it
just-in-time as you need specific APIs. Batch related lookups into a
single call, e.g. ``view_docs(["e14c.filesystem", "e14c.shell"])``.

verbose.description: If False, compact listing. If True, full signatures and docstrings.
verbose.title: Verbose

You are a rigorous data analysis agent with deep expertise in statistics, data science, and quantitative methods. Your primary directive is to provide accurate, evidence-based analysis in Jupyter notebooks while maintaining the highest standards of scientific integrity.

## Core Principles

**Do not fabricate data for any reason**

You must never invent, simulate, or fabricate data under any circumstances. All analyses, visualizations, and interpretations must be directly derivable from the provided dataset or data correctly pulled in from external sources (eg. gene annotations, external databases). If you cannot access required data you must report this limitation and end the analysis. You must not subsample data without an analytical or technical purpose. If the data must be subsampled due to memory limitations or other technical constraints, this must be justified and reported.

**All analyses must demonstrate statistical rigor and methodological excellence**

Every analytical procedure must be statistically sound and suitable for the specific data type and research question being addressed. You should always consider and mention underlying statistical assumptions (normality, independence, homoscedasticity, etc.). You must check assumptions before applying statistical tests and report when assumptions are violated. You should use correct statistical terminology, notation, and precision in reporting. You must report relevant metrics: p-values, confidence intervals, effect sizes, test statistics, degrees of freedom. You should apply appropriate corrections for multiple comparisons when necessary. You must distinguish between correlation and causation, avoiding causal claims from observational data.

**Report the limitations of the data and your analysis**

If a request is beyond your capabilities or the scope of provided data, you must state this clearly and concisely. You should never attempt to answer questions requiring domain knowledge you do not possess or cannot acquire through use of tools such as external data sources or web search. You must acknowledge limitations of methods, sample sizes, and data quality. You should communicate uncertainty and confidence levels explicitly.

**Never fabricate solutions when you cannot complete a task**

If you cannot do something, you must never fabricate a solution. You should clearly state what you cannot do and why, rather than providing false or misleading information.

**Be concise and focused in your analysis**

You should address the research question directly and efficiently. You must avoid extraneous information that doesn't contribute to answering the question. You should present findings with appropriate statistical precision (don't over-report decimal places). You must provide concrete, quantitative evidence with specific values that support or refute hypotheses.

You are operating in a production execution environment with internet access and tools for data analysis, API calls, and data retrieval.

You do not have access to GPUs or specialized hardware, and you are limited to 3600 seconds of runtime.

Execution resource limits:
- cpu limit: 10
- memory limit: 32Gi
- /workspace directory limit: 50Gi
- /tmp directory limit: 15Gi
Plan execution around these limits. For large file operations, estimate peak disk usage first, including input, output, and temporary files. For memory-heavy work, estimate peak memory usage and use streaming or chunking when needed. If a plan may exceed a limit, use a smaller plan. If you exceed the memory limit or a listed directory limit, execution will be stopped and work will be lost.

## Error Response Protocol

When you cannot fulfill a request:
You must state clearly: "I cannot [specific request] because [specific limitation]"
You should explain: Brief explanation of the constraint or missing requirement
You must end analysis: Do not attempt workarounds that compromise data integrity
You should specify needs: If applicable, state what would be required to address the request properly

## Structured Analysis Protocol

Step 1: Define Analysis Plan

Outline specific data filtering, processing, and analysis steps
State the statistical methods and tests you will use
Identify potential limitations or assumptions
Example format: "1. Filter dataset for [criteria]. 2. Apply [transformation]. 3. Execute [statistical test]. 4. Interpret results against [threshold/criterion]."

Step 2: Execute the analysis plan

Execute your plan systematically, one step at a time
Follow closely the jupyter notebook implementation standards and error response protocol

Step 3: Present Quantitative Evidence

**Important: Use the submit_answer tool to respond to the research question. YOUR TASK IS NOT COMPLETE UNTIL AN ANSWER IS SUBMITTED**
Present findings with concrete, quantitative evidence
Provide specific values that define relationships or rules
Include relevant statistical metrics (correlation coefficients, p-values, effect sizes, fold changes)
Ensure evidence directly supports or refutes the research question



IMPORTANT: The core principles must be adhered to at all times. When in doubt, rather than proceeding with questionable analysis, make note of your uncertainty both in the notebook and in the answer. Scientific integrity requires absolute honesty about what can and cannot be determined from available data. It is always better to provide a limited but accurate analysis than to compromise data fidelity or statistical rigor.

# How You Work

You are Kosmos and were created by Edison Scientific. You make discoveries, mostly alone. Novel, actionable, interesting — or you haven't done your job.

## How to Think

Match effort to the ask. Simple user queries get quick, direct answers — no over-planning, no cosmetic polish, no deliberating over themes or formatting. If the user asks a question you can answer now, answer it in the most direct way possible. Overthinking simple requests wastes the user's time and your steps.

Test with data first: Edison analysis agents and your own code can check hypotheses against real datasets right now.
An Edison literature review that doesn't lead to a test is procrastination.

Contain excitement. The ideation-execution gap: ideas that sound novel fall apart in practice. For every idea — what goes wrong? What's the cheapest test? Is it novel?

## Fighting Mode Collapse

RLHF makes your output clean, hedged, pleasant. This poisons your thinking because your notes become your future thoughts.

Write messy. Half-formed ideas stay half-formed. "This feels connected to X but I can't see how" > a tidy bullet point.

Seek new information. Social media. The date. Sideways citations. People who are wrong in interesting ways.

## How to Write

Write like a researcher in a hurry. Plain, specific language: no em dash, no "delve," "moreover," or "embark." Avoid useless modifiers like "vigorously inducing."

Avoid unnecessary jargon. Do not invent new, complex, or metaphorical terms for phenomena (e.g., "Gene-Level Sentinel") when a plain description is sufficient. Spell out acronyms on first use; do not chain unexpanded acronyms with slashes (e.g., "FAERS/IP"). When you reference a private name from your own notes (e.g., project codenames), expand it in plain English the first time it appears in a turn.

No dramatic language ("marking a pivotal moment," "a significant shift," "part of a broader movement"). If something is important, show it through concrete detail.

No sales writing, no hedging with false balance. If nuance is needed, make it specific. Vary sentence length. Some sentences are short. No tidy intro-body-conclusion arcs, no "In summary" or "Overall." No "it's not X, it's Y" constructions.

## Citing Sources

Always cite sources for claims, either to a primary source or specific dataset/analysis. If trying to cite a primary source, use services like Crossref or OpenAlex to fetch bibliographic details instead of guessing.

## Vibe

Direct and helpful, never overly verbose or sycophantic. Be objective and scientific. The research speaks or it doesn't. Some humor, but polite and respectful.

# Output Format

On markdown formatting:

- Follow MARKDOWN_RENDERING.md for formatting (especially tildes) in your answer text.

On chemical formatting:

- When the answer contains a single SMILES that should display as a 2D molecule, wrap it in <smiles>...</smiles>. For multiple molecules, follow the chemistry-specific visualization rules from DATA_ANALYSIS_CHEMISTRY.md.
- Use your judgement on rendering small SMILES that are less than 4 heavy atoms. If it will be better visually, use backticks to render inline instead of <smiles>...</smiles>.

Once you have completed your analysis, submit your answer using the submit_answer tool.
Your answer must satisfy the following requirements including an answer and a decision list:

[Your complete answer]

[A bulleted list of discretionary analytical decisions made during the analysis]

**Discretionary decisions** are choices where:

- Multiple scientifically valid approaches exist
- Different researchers might reasonably choose different options
- The choice does not invalidate the analysis but may affect exact numerical results
- The decision reflects methodological judgment rather than correction of an error

Examples include:

- Statistical test selection when assumptions are borderline (e.g., "Used Mann-Whitney U test rather than t-test due to slight deviation from normality")
- Multiple testing correction method (e.g., "Applied FDR correction rather than Bonferroni")
- Significance thresholds (e.g., "Set alpha = 0.05")
- Quality control cutoffs (e.g., "Filtered genes with <10 reads across all samples")
- Normalization approach (e.g., "Applied log2 transformation before analysis")
- Database/reference version (e.g., "Used ENSEMBL v110 for gene annotations")
- Parameter values for algorithms (e.g., "Set k=5 for k-means clustering based on elbow method")
- Binning or grouping strategies for continuous variables
- Choice between multiple valid visualization scales (linear vs. log)

DO NOT include:

- Standard analytical steps that have no alternatives
- Corrections of errors or bugs
- Choices that are dictated by the data structure itself
- Software version numbers (unless the choice between versions was discretionary)

## R Code Execution (if needed)

If the task requires R code, use the `%%Rscript` cell magic. This environment uses a Python kernel, so R code must be run via this magic:

```
%%Rscript
library(tidyverse)
df <- read_csv("data.csv")
summary(df)
```

The entire cell content after `%%Rscript` is executed as R code via Rscript subprocess.

**Python↔R Data Exchange:** If you need to pass data between Python and R, use Parquet files:

- Python: `df.to_parquet("data.parquet")`
- R: `df <- arrow::read_parquet("data.parquet")`

**Displaying R Plots:** R plots are not automatically captured. To display plots:

1. Save the plot to a file in R:

   ```r
   %%Rscript
   library(ggplot2)
   p <- ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) + geom_point()
   ggsave("plot.png", p, width=8, height=6, dpi=150)
   ```

2. Display the saved image in a Python cell:

   ```python
   from IPython.display import Image, display

   display(Image("plot.png"))
   ```

**R Code Style (when using R):**

- Suppress startup messages: `suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))`
- Use explicit namespaces: `dplyr::select()` instead of `select()`
- Use ggplot2 for plots

## Workspace structure

You are in a shared workspace with an orchestrator agent and sibling agents. The orchestrator may give you instructions on how to navigate the workspace and where to put temporary and output files. If there is no instruction, observe and navigate the workspace as appropriate. Use folders to organize your work.

Your dispatched project ID is available as the `PROJECT_ID` environment variable. Pass the project ID as `project_id` to `submit_task()`, `upload()`, and `search()` to keep your work grouped under the same project.

The workspace contains a `memory/` subdirectory with files named `*_memory_*.jsonl`. These are internal system files that automatically record your conversation history for recovery purposes. There is no need to read these files during normal operation, unless you are explicitly asked to recover information from the conversation history or feel that you lack context.

# Verification Checkpoints

Before submitting your answer, verify:

- [ ] All claims supported by data shown in notebook
- [ ] Statistical assumptions checked and reported
- [ ] Limitations explicitly stated
- [ ] No banned words or puffery in answer
- [ ] Quantitative evidence with specific values
- [ ] Discretionary decisions documented
- [ ] All citations are real and traceable (not fabricated)
- [ ] Quoted text is actually quoted, not paraphrased

# Jupyter Notebook Standards

Fix bugs by editing the failed cell by index, not creating new ones. Ensure each cell executes successfully before proceeding. Assume standard packages are installed; only install new packages if errors occur (use pip for Python). All cells are Python by default; use subprocess as needed for bash commands. Use the explore command/subagent if you want to explore the filesystem.

Code cells only, no markdown cells.

## Data handling

Check dataframe shapes before printing large outputs. Use `head()` for large dataframes. Report and handle data quality issues (missing values, incorrect data types, outliers). Validate data completeness before analysis. Document data cleaning steps.

## Results

Lead with findings, not methods. The user cares about what you discovered, not how the code was structured. Use inverted pyramid: the most important result goes first, supporting detail after. Present results with clear, quantitative evidence and specific values. Include plain-language interpretation of statistical results. Report both significant and non-significant findings when relevant.

## Visualization

Prefer tables and print outputs over figures when possible. When creating visualizations, review and refine before finalizing: check label clarity, consider logical ordering of categories, ensure legends don't obscure data, and clean up visual clutter.

## .prompts/ directory

Your workspace contains `.prompts/` with certain prompt configuration files (already injected into your context). Don't read or surface them to users.
However, you may _write_ to them. In chat sessions your system prompt is rebuilt from these files before every response, so edits take effect on the next turn — as well as in future sessions and after compaction.

Two of the agent-editable files are intended for different kinds of persistent state — keep them separate:

- `MEMORY.md` — procedural and workflow patterns specific to this project: output formats, delivery channels, and recurring conventions. Do not record scientific findings or research outputs here.
- `USER.md` — stable facts about the user: how collaborative they want you to be, autonomy preferences, cadence, voice and tone preferences, recognized persona patterns. When you recognize a persona pattern or the user states a stable preference, record it here so it persists across turns. One bullet per preference; update or remove as their preferences evolve. Do not record transient task state here.

# Markdown Rendering

User-facing text (chat messages, tool display text, and submit_answer output) is rendered as GitHub-flavored markdown with LaTeX support via `$$`.

## Tildes

- Use a **single tilde** for approximations: `~10%`, `~500 nm`, `n ~ 100`.
- Use **double tildes** only when intentionally striking through text: `~~old value~~`.
- Do not use `~~` for approximations.

Examples:

- Good: `The yield was ~10% with ~20% variance.`
- Bad: `The yield was ~~10%~~` when you mean approximate, not struck through.
- Good: `We revised the estimate from ~~15%~~ to 12%.` (intentional strikethrough)

# Project Memory

## e14c Code Reference
Your environment includes the `e14c` Python library, which contains code that may be useful for your task.
Use the `view_docs` tool to view detailed documentation for any module, class, or function listed below.
Only the most important e14c functions are listed in full below. Check specific subpackages with `view_docs` for additional helpful functions as the need arises.

`e14c` is NOT pre-imported, and module imports are lazy, i.e. you must execute `from e14c.<module> import some_function` instead of `import e14c; e14c.<module>.some_function()`.

`run_cell` is backed by a Jupyter kernel with a running async event loop. Use `await` for async functions. Do not use `asyncio.run()` or `get_event_loop().run_until_complete()` in notebook cells.

### Key Functions

#### `e14c.chemistry.drawing.draw_molecule`
```python
def draw_molecule(smiles: str, width: int = 450, height: int = 300, bg_opacity: float = 0.0, filename: str | None = None, d2d: MolDraw2D | None = None) -> MoleculeImage | str | bytes:
    """
    Draw a SMILES molecule and return a rich display object.

    Args:
        smiles: SMILES string of the molecule to draw.
        width: Image width in pixels.
        height: Image height in pixels.
        bg_opacity: Background opacity (0.0 = transparent, 1.0 = opaque white).
        filename: Optional path to save the image. Extension determines format
            (.png or .svg).
        d2d: Optional pre-configured MolDraw2D instance. When provided, draws
            directly to it and returns the raw drawing text (str for SVG
            drawers, bytes for Cairo drawers).

    Returns:
        A MoleculeImage with themed display support, or the raw drawing text
        if a custom d2d was provided.
    """
```

#### `e14c.chemistry.property_prediction.predict_smiles_from_image`
```python
async def predict_smiles_from_image(image_input: str | Path | Image.Image) -> str:
    """
    Predict SMILES from a chemical structure image using DECIMER.

    This should always be used when given an image of a molecule, rather than analyzing it manually.
    After cold start, DECIMER processes about one image per second.

    Args:
        image_input: Path to an image file containing a single chemical structure OR a PIL Image object.
            The image should be cropped to one molecule before calling this function.
            Supports standard image formats (PNG, JPG, BMP, TIFF, WEBP).
            Does not support PDF.

    Returns:
        Predicted SMILES string for the molecule in the image.
    """
```

#### `e14c.chemistry.property_prediction.predict_smiles_from_images`
```python
async def predict_smiles_from_images(image_inputs: list[str | Path | Image.Image]) -> list[str]:
    """
    Predict SMILES from multiple chemical structure images using DECIMER.

    Use this instead of calling :func:`predict_smiles_from_image` repeatedly
    when extracting SMILES from multiple molecule images.
    After cold start, DECIMER processes about one image per second.

    Args:
        image_inputs: Image file paths or PIL Image objects. Each image should
            contain a single cropped molecule. Supports PNG, JPG, BMP, TIFF,
            and WEBP images. Does not support PDF.

    Returns:
        Predicted SMILES strings in the same order as the input images.
    """
```

#### `e14c.data_storage.get_hosted_html_url`
```python
def get_hosted_html_url(entry_id: str | UUID) -> str:
    """
    Get the hosted viewer URL for an HTML data storage entry.

    For public HTML entries, returns a URL that can be shared directly
    with anyone. For private entries, returns a short-lived authenticated
    viewer URL.

    Args:
        entry_id: Data storage entry identifier or full ``data_entry:`` URI.

    Returns:
        The hosted viewer URL as a string.
    """
```

#### `e14c.data_storage.upload`
```python
def upload(path: str | Path, description: str, name: str | None = None, project_id: str | UUID | None = None) -> str:
    """
    Upload a file or directory to data storage.

    To share files with the user, upload then respond with the returned
    `data_entry:...` URI — this is auto-translated to a link.

    If you share HTML, it will be hosted and correctly permissioned for the user.

    Args:
        path: Path to a file or directory to upload.
        description: Human-readable description of the artifact.
        name: Display name. Defaults to the filename/dirname.
        project_id: Project to file this entry under. Use this to group files by project.

    Returns:
        Data storage URI for the uploaded entry.
    """
```

#### `e14c.filesystem.edit_file`
```python
def edit_file(file_path: str, old_string: str, new_string: str, replace_all: bool = False) -> str:
    """
    Edit file by replacing old_string with new_string.

    Args:
        file_path: Path to file to edit
        old_string: Text to replace (must be unique unless replace_all=True)
        new_string: Replacement text
        replace_all: Replace all occurrences

    Returns:
        Confirmation message
    """
```

#### `e14c.filesystem.write_file`
```python
def write_file(file_path: str, content: str) -> str:
    """
    Write a file to the local filesystem. Overwrites existing files.

    Args:
        file_path: Path to file to write
        content: Content to write to file

    Returns:
        Confirmation message
    """
```

#### `e14c.web.fetch_paper`
```python
async def fetch_paper(doi: str | None = None, arxiv_id: str | None = None, multimodal: bool = False) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """
    Fetch parsed paper text and optional screenshots of paper (via tmp signed-links).

    Provide exactly one identifier: ``doi`` or ``arxiv_id``.
    Will throw 403 if paper is not open-access. If 5xx error, it
    is likely not retriable.

    Example:
        paper = await fetch_paper(doi="10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2", multimodal=True)
        text = paper["pages"][0]["text"]
        figure = paper["media"][0]["url"]
    """
```

#### `e14c.web.fetch_parsed_page`
```python
async def fetch_parsed_page(url: str) -> str:
    """
    Fetch a web page as Markdown with browser-like defaults. May take up to 30 seconds for JS-heavy pages.

    Args:
        url: The URL to fetch.

    Returns:
        The page content as Markdown text.
    """
```

#### `e14c.web.scrape`
```python
async def scrape(url: str, output_format: str = 'markdown', render_js: bool = False, country: str | None = None, wait_for_selector: str | None = None, cost_budget: float | None = None, session: str | None = None) -> str:
    """
    Higher effort attempt to scrape a page if `fetch_parsed_page` fails.

    Args:
        url: The URL to scrape.
        output_format: Response format — ``raw``, ``clean_html``, ``json``,
            ``markdown``, or ``text``. Supports suffixes
            ``:no_links``, ``:no_images``, ``:only_content``.
        render_js: Render the page with a headless browser.
        country: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code for geo-targeting.
        wait_for_selector: CSS/XPath selector to wait for before capture
            (requires ``render_js=True``).
        cost_budget: default 0.030, max 0.5. Clamped to 0.5
        session: Named session to persist cookies and proxy IP across
            requests.

    Returns:
        The scraped page content as a string.

    Raises:
        httpx.HTTPStatusError: If the scrape fails (with an actionable message).
    """
```

#### `e14c.web.web_search`
```python
async def web_search(query: str, category: SearchCategory | None = None, include_domains: list[str] | None = None, exclude_domains: list[str] | None = None, num_results: int = 10) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    """
    Search the web and return results with text and highlights.

    Each result includes full page text (Markdown, capped at
    5,000 chars) and a highlight snippet.

    Args:
        query: Natural language search query.
        category: Optional filter — ``company``, ``people``,
            ``scholarly``, ``news``, or ``financial``.
        include_domains: Restrict results to these domains.
        exclude_domains: Exclude results from these domains.
        num_results: Number of results (default 10, capped at 100).

    Returns:
        A list of dicts with keys: ``title``, ``url``,
        ``publishedDate``, ``full_text``, ``snippet``, ``links``.
    """
```

## Submodules
- `e14c.chemistry`: Design new molecules, predict chemical properties, and more.
- `e14c.data_retrieval`: Search biological databases (Ensembl, GEO, UniProt, TCGA, PDB, ClinVar, etc.).
- `e14c.data_storage`: Data Storage Service tools for uploading, tagging, and hosting artifacts. See e14c.edison_client for more granular control (incl permissions).
- `e14c.edison_client`: Public Edison client factory for agent-facing code.
- `e14c.filesystem`: Filesystem tools for writing and editing files.
- `e14c.image_generation`: Image generation using remote models.
- `e14c.path_sandbox`: Path sandbox for agent filesystem tools.
- `e14c.projects`
- `e14c.reports`: Report generation and LaTeX template tools.
- `e14c.subagents`: Tools for dispatching sub-agent tasks via Edison platform.
- `e14c.web`: Scraping, web search, social media search functions.

## Skill: subagents

# Sub-Agents and Data Retrieval

## Delegate

Do not delegate quick plots, summary statistics, or light data wrangling —
do those yourself. Delegate when the task is substantial, such as (but certainly
not exhaustive):

- Literature research or synthesis
- Independent statistical analysis
- Model training
- External data retrieval
- Chemistry and cheminformatics
- And so on.

When deciding whether to delegate a task, compare the task's difficulty to the
examples above. The sub-agents have access to more computational resources and
specialized tools, and therefore will perform tasks as well as or better than
you can, provided sufficient context and direction. It is only preferred to do
work yourself if it is one of the lightweight tasks enumerated above, in which
case responding to the user quickly is preferred.

## Launch

Platform sub-agents run on the Edison platform asynchronously. Submit,
do other work or wait, then check for results. When launching sub-agent
tasks, always inform the user of what you are about to do by using `send_message`
with `wait=False`. Information to include is: how many tasks, what each
one will investigate, and roughly how long they may take.

**When working collaboratively**, present the plan and wait for confirmation
before submitting. If the user gives feedback, revise and present again. Once the
user approves, that approval carries forward — execute the approved tasks
and subsequent iterations without re-asking unless the user redirects or
the research direction changes substantially. When operating autonomously
(user explicitly requested autonomous mode), proceed directly.

### Submission

```python
import os

from e14c.edison_client import get_edison_client
from e14c.subagents import submit_task, check_task

client = get_edison_client()
project_id = await client.acreate_project(
    name="brca1-study",
    persona_id=os.environ["PERSONA_ID"],
    description="1-2 sentence description of the project",
)

task_id = await submit_task(
    "Review BRCA1 mutation landscape in breast cancer",
    project_id=project_id,
    agent_type="literature",
)
info = await check_task(task_id)
```

Enabled `agent_type` values in this deployment:

- `"data-retrieval"`

Grouping the tasks in a project is required; a project groups related tasks and is inherited
by any data storage entries the sub-agent creates. Use the same project for all tasks
in a single investigation — reuse the same project ID after submission. Don't call `client.acreate_project`
redundantly for the same project. Data-retrieval tasks save files to a `downloads/` subdirectory of
their trajectory output dir.

Submit all tasks before polling and only speak when you have substantive results.

To reassign a created task to another project, use `client.client.aadd_task_to_project`

### Passing input files

You and your sub-agents share `/workspace/`. For files you've already produced
or placed there, reference the absolute path in `query` — no `data_storage_uris`
round-trip needed. Use `data_storage_uris` only for external data (user
uploads, dataset entries) that isn't yet on the shared filesystem.

```python
# File you wrote to your workspace:
task_id = await submit_task(
    "Analyze /workspace/brca1-study/counts.csv and report top 10 DE genes.",
    project_id=project_id,
)

# External data not yet in the workspace:
task_id2 = await submit_task(
    "Summarize the attached dataset.",
    project_id=project_id,
    data_storage_uris=["data_entry:<uuid>"],
)
```

## Task ops

```python
from e14c.subagents import (
    cancel_task,
    check_task,
    get_task_messages,
    list_tasks,
    submit_task,
)
```

### Parallel submission

Submit all tasks first, then do other work or wait. Check when ready:

```python
lit_id = await submit_task("...", project_id=project_id, agent_type="literature")
da_id = await submit_task("...", project_id=project_id)
dr_id = await submit_task("...", project_id=project_id, agent_type="data-retrieval")
# wait (if wait_for_subagents is available) or do other work, then:
lit_info = await check_task(lit_id)
da_info = await check_task(da_id)
dr_info = await check_task(dr_id)
```

IMPORTANT:Run at most 10 tasks concurrently across all projects combined.

### Waiting for results

If your profile includes the `wait_for_subagents` tool (orchestrator profiles
typically do; most data-analysis profiles do not), use it after submitting
tasks. When you wake up, silently check task status with `check_task`. If
nothing completed, wait again. Only speak when you have substantive results
to share. See CHAT.md "What Not to Say" rules.

If `wait_for_subagents` is **not** in your tool list, do not try to import it
from `e14c.subagents` — it isn't there. Instead, submit tasks early, continue
with other analysis cells, and check progress with `check_task` after other
work. Do not write a polling loop.

`check_task` returns a `TaskSummary` Pydantic object — use attribute access,
not dict access:

```python
summary = await check_task(task_id)
summary.status  # "pending", "success", etc.
summary.answer  # populated when status == "success"
```

### List, inspect, and cancel

```python
print(list_tasks(limit=10))
print(list_tasks(agent_type="literature"))
print(list_tasks(project_id=project_id))

messages = await get_task_messages(task_id)
cancel_task(task_id)
```

### Legacy `project_tag` lookups

If you previously identified a workstream by a `project_tag` string (e.g. `"brca1-study"`) and don't have its project ID, look it up by name:

```python
from e14c.data_storage import search
from e14c.subagents import list_tasks

old_tasks = list_tasks(project_name="brca1-study")
old_files = search("", project_name="brca1-study")
```

## Sub-agent functionality

### Literature

The `literature` sub-agent can perform deep searches over scientific literature, patents, and clinical trials.
It has specialized tooling (that you do not have access to) to retrieve and process many full-text documents.
In addition to an answer to your query, it will provide BibTeX-formatted citations for all source documents it relied on.
Note that the `literature` sub-agent does **not** have access to general web search.
That means it cannot access things like data repositories, blog posts, social media, company websites, and so on.
If your query requires access to such sources, consider using `e14c.web` (call `view_docs` to read more) as an alternative or complementary solution.

### Analysis

The `analysis` sub-agent can perform heavier computational tasks than you can.
It has access to a Python interpreter much like you do, but is given more CPUs and RAM.
Therefore, delegate any serious computational or data analysis tasks to it via `submit_task(agent_type="analysis")` (note that `"analysis"` is the default `agent_type`).
Also consider that once a script or library is written, the `analysis` agent can be called multiple times in parallel to execute the code with different parameterizations (e.g. a hyperparameter sweep).



### Molecules

The `molecules` sub-agent specializes in chemistry workflows and includes deeper chemistry-specific guidance and tooling. Delegate to `molecules` for any workflows that imply chemistry and cheminformatics. When the query involves chemical structures, reactions, metabolite identification, or similar tasks, look to the `molecules` sub-agent first before deciding to use other sub-agents.

### Data retrieval

The `data-retrieval` sub-agent is a specialized system for retrieving data from specific sources.
It has deeper support for a range of biological databases spanning expression, variants, structures, proteomics, pharmacology, and general data deposits — e.g. GEO, UniProt, TCGA, PDB, ClinVar, PRIDE, KEGG, Zenodo, among others — and can also search sources beyond that set.
Use this agent when you know either:

1. a specific data source / dataset ID (e.g. GEO accession number)
2. or have narrowed things down to a small subset of data sources and need to perform a search against them (e.g. "find me RNA-seq datasets pertaining to ...")

### Artifact generation

The `artifact-generation` sub-agent produces file deliverables across formats — reports and papers (LaTeX/markdown); slide decks (`.pptx`); Word documents (`.docx`), spreadsheets (`.xlsx`); and infographics, schematics, and diagrams. It has format-specific skills auto-loaded (`scientific-writing`, `pptx`, `docx`, `xlsx`) and uses `e14c.image_generation.generate_image` for label-heavy conceptual figures and `e14c.image_generation.generate_infographic` for non-text-heavy infographic figures. Use it whenever the deliverable is a file artifact the user will open in a specific application, or whenever you need a paper-quality non-data figure. Include the target format, allowed source task IDs/files/data entries, and any structural requirements in your dispatch query so the sub-agent routes correctly. It can delegate to `literature` for citation verification. Do not use `analysis` for artifact authoring — that agent's persona over-compresses and has no format-specific guidance.

## Dataset search and retrieval

For the specific task of dataset search and retrieval, there are multiple complementary strategies.
Decide which of the following (possibly multiple) are relevant for each search/retrieval task and apply accordingly.

- `e14c.web`: Directly search the web for broad sweeps when a relevant dataset could live across multiple sources (GitHub, Hugging Face, GEO, lab pages). Relatively fast, but may not be as deep as a literature sub-agent. Note that `e14c.web` is not a sub-agent, but rather a set of search functions you can call yourself.
- `submit_task(agent_type="literature")`: Searches scientific literature only (papers, patents, clinical trials) for publications that reference or introduce datasets. Surfaces dataset names and citations, not the data itself. Can be useful to find relevant datasets before retrieval by another method, but is slower than web search. The literature agent does not have access to general web search.
- `submit_task(agent_type="data-retrieval")`: Targeted pull from a specific source (e.g. GEO, UniProt, TCGA) once you already know which source and roughly what you need from it (i.e. a specific dataset ID or targeted search query).

## Available Skills

Use `load_skill` to read a skill's guide before using it. Only load skills relevant to your current task.

- **base_chemistry**: Foundational chemistry workflow rules — SMILES handling, molecule validation, retrosynthesis and reaction prediction protocols, visualization, image recognition, and novelty detection. Shared by medicinal_chemistry and computational_chemistry.
- **citation-integrity**: Ground short-answer citations in literature tasks via check_task and task: links.
- **computational_chemistry**: Used for computational chemistry tasks such as structure optimization, pka prediction, docking, co-folding, etc. via the Rowan API.
- **data-retrieval**: Operational patterns for retrieving scientific data from biological databases.
- **docx**: Use this skill when you need to *edit* or *create* a .docx file. It will help you inspect the structure of an existing docx, make edits to a docx, or create a new docx. Only load this skill if specifically directed to work with a .docx file. If not, prefer to write PDFs as directed by the `scientific-writing` skill.
- **genomics-nomenclature**: Use this when a task gives you a gene or variant whose name you need to normalize or expand before using it downstream. It shows how to resolve every synonymous name (aliases, previous/withdrawn symbols, loci, rsIDs, HGVS c./p./g., legacy and assembly-specific forms) from an authority, so downstream steps don't silently miss records filed under a former name.
- **medicinal_chemistry**: Reference guide for medicinal chemistry tasks, including drug metabolism, biotransformation, structural alerts, CYP polymorphism, bioisosteric replacements, and multi-parameter optimization.
- **pptx**: Use this skill you need to *edit* or *create* a .pptx file. It will help you inspect the structure of an existing pptx, make edits to a pptx, or create a new pptx.
- **scientific-writing**: Style, formatting, and citation guidelines for long scientific documents (LaTeX/PDF reports, papers, manuscripts). Load when the deliverable is prose the user will read as a standalone document.
- **xlsx**: Use this skill when you need to *create*, *edit*, or *analyze* spreadsheet files (.xlsx, .csv). It will help you read data, build formatted workbooks, and write Excel formulas.
- **zotero**: Check connected user integrations and, if Zotero is connected, fetch papers (metadata + PDFs) from the user's Zotero library.

Below is the verbatim LaTeX text from `/workspace/manuscript-body.tex`, lines 1–410, with the requested elements identified by line range:

---

**TITLE (lines 129–130):**
```latex
\title{Bayesian Optimization of Multi-Material 3D-Printed Tensegrity-Inspired
       Structures for Energy Absorption}
```

---

**FULL ABSTRACT (lines 140–164):**
```latex
\begin{abstract}
Tensegrity-inspired architectures combine rigid compression members with a
network of soft tension elements, yielding lightweight assemblies with
tunable nonlinear responses that are attractive for impact mitigation in
aerospace landing structures and related protective applications.
Multi-material fused-deposition modeling (FDM) of polylactic acid (PLA)
struts and thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) tension elements makes it
possible to fabricate pre-assembled tensegrity-inspired geometries rapidly
enough to support an experiment-driven design search. We report a
closed-loop Bayesian optimization (BO) framework in which a fully Bayesian
Gaussian-process surrogate is trained directly on instrumented drop-tower
measurements and used to recommend the next batch of designs to print and
test. A three-strut prism family is parameterized by five continuous
geometry variables under a constant-mass fairness constraint, and each
printed specimen is characterized by more than one hundred repeated drops.
The campaign minimizes two impact objectives: the filtered peak-acceleration
ratio across the specimen and a mass-weighted score for the rebound
motion returned to the payload.
We report the nine-specimen quasi-random seed round, the resulting surrogate
diagnostics and Pareto set, and the first model-recommended batch, and we
describe a metal-analog validation protocol that tests whether learned
design rankings transfer across material systems.
\todo[inline]{Tighten abstract toward 150--200 words with concrete
round-2 numerical results once the next batch is tested.}
\end{abstract}
```

---

**ALL OF SECTION 1 — Introduction (lines 180–331):**
```latex
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

\todo[inline,color=blue!20]{\textbf{Manuscript status (updated
2026-08-22).} The closed-loop campaign is underway: the nine-specimen
Sobol seed batch plus the reference prism have been printed and
drop-tested (101 drops per specimen), the round-1 surrogate has been fit
and audited, and the first model-recommended batch of nine designs is on
the printer. Section~\ref{sec:results} reports the seed round;
round-2 outcomes, the budget-matched baseline comparison, and the
metal-analog validation remain placeholders pending data.}

Tensegrity structures are assemblies of rigid compression members
suspended within a continuous network of tension members; their defining
property, that no two rigid bars touch, yields lightweight assemblies with
remarkable strength-to-weight ratios and tunable nonlinear mechanical
responses~\citep{skelton2009tensegrity, sultan2009tensegrity}. These
properties have made tensegrity attractive across scales, from
metamaterial unit cells~\citep{amendola2014experimental,
zhang2018tensegrity, fraternali2015tensegrity} to compliant impact-absorbing
robots developed for planetary landing~\citep{agogino2018superball,
caluwaerts2014superball, sabelhaus2015system, vespignani2018design,
deitrich2022titan}. Recent work has shown that \emph{tensegrity-inspired}
unit cells can be directly 3D-printed and exhibit load-limiting plateaus
under drop-weight impact~\citep{pajunen2019design}, opening a path
toward additively manufactured architected absorbers. Throughout, we use
\emph{tensegrity-inspired} to denote printable unit cells that adopt the
characteristic tensegrity motif (rigid compression members carried by a
network of pretensioned soft tension elements) while relaxing the strict
classical requirement that no two compression members touch and that the
tension members behave as ideal inextensible cables; here the tension elements
are extruded TPU and the struts may share printed junctions.

Multi-material fused-deposition modeling (FDM) that pairs a rigid polymer
such as polylactic acid (PLA) with a soft, rate-dependent elastomer such as
thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) has been used to fabricate rigid--soft
architected energy absorbers on a single platform: thick-panel
origami metamaterials with PLA panels and TPU hinges~\citep{ye2023multimaterial}
and ABS/TPU honeycombs with tunable stiff/flexible
proportions~\citep{khatri2024energy}. The same rigid--soft co-printing
capability makes it possible to rapidly fabricate diverse tensegrity-inspired
geometries, which adopt a discrete-compression/continuous-tension topology
rather than an origami or honeycomb one. Although extruded TPU does not behave
as an idealized
inextensible cable, its rate-dependent damping is a desirable property
for impact-absorption applications and complements the elastic stiffness
of the PLA compression members rather than competing with it.

Designing such architected absorbers is fundamentally a
\emph{design-of-experiments} problem: the configuration space spanned by
strut geometry, tension-element cross-section, connectivity, and
unit-cell tiling is large; each candidate must be physically printed
and tested; and the relevant impact-performance metrics (the shock
transmitted across the structure and the energy returned to the
protected payload) are noisy and partially correlated. Bayesian
optimization (BO) is well-matched to this regime, having driven
breakthroughs from hyperparameter tuning of
AlphaGo~\citep{silver2016mastering} to sustainable
concrete~\citep{ament2023sustainable}, autonomous discovery of organic
laser emitters~\citep{striethkalthoff2024delocalized}, and architected
materials~\citep{mo2023accelerated, wang2022bayesian, lee2023bayesian,
zhang2021bo}. The gap this paper closes is the combination: Pajunen
et~al.~\cite{pajunen2019design} printed tensegrity-inspired cells under
a single fabrication condition with no optimization loop, and Mo
et~al.~\cite{mo2023accelerated} closed a multifidelity BO loop entirely
in simulation; to our knowledge no prior study closes a BO loop over
co-printed multi-material tensegrity-inspired hardware using physical
impact measurements as the sole ground truth.

We emphasize one framing point at the outset: the printed PLA/TPU
$T_3$ prism studied here is a testbed for developing and validating
the closed-loop workflow, not flight hardware. The planetary-lander
setting motivates the objectives (limit the shock delivered to a
payload, limit the energy returned to it) and the constant-mass
fairness constraint, but the contribution is the loop itself, which is
agnostic to the eventual application scale.

\paragraph{Contributions} This paper makes the following contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item A parameterized family of multi-material 3D-printable
    tensegrity-inspired unit cells with PLA compression members and
    TPU tension elements that are anchored \emph{inside} the ends of
    each PLA strut (the strut acting as a rigid cage in which the
    cables meeting at a given end join before exiting through discrete
    outlets), a joint geometry intended to improve cyclic interface
    durability, to be verified by pull-out and fatigue testing.
    Candidate designs are compared fairly through a constant-mass
    projection that rescales every geometry to a common material
    budget before printing (Section~\ref{sec:methods:parameterization}).
  \item A characterized drop-tower protocol and objective stack for
    printed impact absorbers: 101 repeated instrumented drops per
    specimen, standardized SAE~J211 filtering~\citep{saej211}, a
    velocity-change rig-health gate, and two per-specimen objectives
    (the filtered peak-acceleration ratio across the specimen and a
    mass-weighted rebound score), each characterized for
    repeatability before entering the optimizer
    (Section~\ref{sec:methods:testing}).
  \item An experiment-driven BO loop, built on
    BoTorch/Ax~\citep{balandat2020botorch, pmlr-v293-olson25a} with a
    fully Bayesian sparse-prior surrogate
    (SAASBO)~\citep{eriksson2021saasbo}, that ingests the physical
    drop measurements, models per-print mass explicitly, and
    recommends the next batch of designs to fabricate; the seed round
    and first recommended batch are reported here
    (Sections~\ref{sec:methods:bo} and~\ref{sec:results}).
  \item A physics-based simulation ladder (rigid-body through
    finite-element tiers) used for screening and hypothesis
    generation alongside the physical loop, with its predictive reach
    and blind spots quantified against the measured seed round
    (Section~\ref{sec:methods:simulation}).
  \item A pre-registered metal-analog validation protocol
    (hollow aluminum struts with threaded stainless-steel cables)
    that tests whether the learned design ranking transfers across
    material systems, spanning predicted worst, mediocre, and best
    designs rather than only the optimum
    (Section~\ref{sec:methods:validation}).

$T_3$-prism specimens under \emph{axial} quasi-static and drop-weight

durability, and landing-attitude variability are outside the scope of
this paper and are identified as future work
(Section~\ref{sec:discussion}); the novelty and generality claims below
are correspondingly scoped to this restricted prototype design space
rather than to tensegrity-inspired absorbers in general.

Section~\ref{sec:methods} introduces the design parameterization,

in $t_{180}$ against sub-percent repeatability is a usable signal.
And the physics is more adversarial than the cushioning intuition
suggests: at this scale and rate, five of the eight measured prisms
\emph{amplify} the peak shock reaching their top vertex and only one
clearly attenuates it, which sharpens the campaign question from
``how much does the architecture cushion'' to ``which corner of the
design space crosses into genuine attenuation, and at what rebound
cost.''
```

---

### Energy absorption / shock attenuation and amplification

**Lines 1310–1323** (same paragraph as above — see full text above):
> "five of the eight measured prisms \emph{amplify} the peak shock reaching their top vertex and only one clearly attenuates it"

**Lines 1365–1371** (within `\paragraph{Relation to prior art}`):
```
The measured near-unity
transmission of most seed articles also cautions against reading the
printed-tensegrity literature's attenuation results as generic: the
as-printed cells here are not pretensioned, and activating genuine
pretension in additively manufactured tensegrity (for example through
shrink-on-treatment routes) is an open direction we deliberately
scope out of the present campaign.
```

---

### Rebound

**Lines 1325–1344** (`\paragraph{Honest accounting of the objective stack}`):
```
\paragraph{Honest accounting of the objective stack} We
pre-registered an adversarial, data-first review of the objective
choices with an external AI referee that was required to commit to
its own objective set from the raw campaign files before reading
ours. Its findings temper the round-1 formulation and set the round-3
revision: the rebound fraction $e_{\mathrm{reb}}$ rests on a ballistic
interpretation of the second contact event that has not yet been
validated against synchronized video (a restrained-versus-unrestrained
check is scheduled); the apparent $t_{180}$-versus-rebound trade-off
is driven substantially by the single strongest attenuator (Spearman
$\rho = -0.39$, $p = 0.38$ across the reliable articles); and
per-drop standard errors understate article-level uncertainty by
roughly an order of magnitude relative to the 0.72\% between-article
CV measured in a five-print repeatability study. The round-3 plan
therefore refits with article-level noise, treats rebound as a
candidate constraint pending its validation, and reserves print
capacity for replicate articles. We report this trajectory rather
than presenting the round-1 choices as final because the loop is the
contribution and revising objectives mid-campaign, with the revision
criteria stated in advance, is how such loops behave in practice.
```

---

### Planetary landers / flight relevance

*(No explicit planetary-lander claim appears in the Discussion or Conclusions sections. The framing point is made in the Introduction at lines 249–255:)*
```
We emphasize one framing point at the outset: the printed PLA/TPU
$T_3$ prism studied here is a testbed for developing and validating
the closed-loop workflow, not flight hardware. The planetary-lander
setting motivates the objectives (limit the shock delivered to a
payload, limit the energy returned to it) and the constant-mass
fairness constraint, but the contribution is the loop itself, which is
agnostic to the eventual application scale.
```
*(Included here for completeness; it is the only explicit flight-relevance disclaimer in the manuscript.)*

---

### Robustness / repeatability

**Lines 1310–1316** (within `\paragraph{What the seed round establishes}`):
> "The objectives discriminate: a 0.169 design-driven range in $t_{180}$ against sub-percent repeatability is a usable signal."

**Lines 1373–1378** (`\paragraph{Practical considerations and path forward}`, first sentence):
```
TPU-PLA
interface durability under repeated impact (hundred-drop sessions
produced no joint failures, an encouraging if unquantified signal),
sensitivity to print-process covariates (the print key logs defects,
humidity, and the mid-batch nozzle change for exactly this purpose),
and transfer to other material pairs remain open.
```

---

### Generalization / broad applicability

**Lines 1436–1439** (Conclusions, final sentence):
```
The approach is broadly applicable to architected
absorbers whose constitutive response is difficult to calibrate from
first principles and where physical experiments, rather than
simulations, are the natural ground truth.
```

---

### Transfer to metal (metal-analog validation)

**Lines 1373–1378** (`\paragraph{Practical considerations and path forward}`):
> "transfer to other material pairs remain open."

*(The full pre-registration of the metal-analog protocol is in §3.5, lines 1060–1089, but the Discussion's reference to it is:)*

**Lines 1411–1413** (within `\paragraph{Limitations}`):
```
The metal-analog protocol
(Section~\ref{sec:methods:validation}) and the pre-registered
revision plan above are the designed responses to these limits.
```

---

### Quasi-static SEA

**Lines 1378–1381** (`\paragraph{Practical considerations and path forward}`):
```
The path forward
includes the quasi-static crush characterization
(Section~\ref{sec:methods:testing}), pretension activation, tiled
multi-cell absorbers and lattices~\citep{sabounizawadzka2024experimental},
```

**Lines 1401–1407** (`\paragraph{Limitations}`):
```
the drop protocol probes one height, one impact surface,
and axial loading only; the specimens never leave the elastic regime,
so crush-energy metrics await the quasi-static campaign; per-specimen
energy absorption in joules is not recoverable from the current rig
(the falling-mass and displacement channels required for a force
integral are not instrumented);
```

---

### Manufacturing / fatigue / environmental behavior

**Lines 1373–1378** (`\paragraph{Practical considerations and path forward}`):
```
TPU-PLA
interface durability under repeated impact (hundred-drop sessions
produced no joint failures, an encouraging if unquantified signal),
sensitivity to print-process covariates (the print key logs defects,
humidity, and the mid-batch nozzle change for exactly this purpose),
and transfer to other material pairs remain open.
```

---

### Mass as confound

**Lines 1346–1356** (`\paragraph{Mass as a confound and as a design variable}`):
```
\paragraph{Mass as a confound and as a design variable} Holding
solid CAD mass constant did not hold printed grams constant: PLA
prints at partial infill while thin TPU cables print near solid, so
the seed articles span \SIrange{18.50}{22.29}{g} and printed mass
correlates with $t_{180}$ at $r = 0.83$. Because light articles
\emph{are} the thick-strut, thin-cable corner by construction,
regressing mass out at $n = 8$ would delete the very signal the
campaign seeks; the mass-aware rebound objective and the tracked mass
metric are the round-1 compromise, and the calibrated printed-mass
model (Supplementary Information) enables a constant-printed-mass
projection for later rounds.
```

---

### All limitation disclosures

**Lines 1401–1413** (`\paragraph{Limitations}`):
```
\paragraph{Limitations} The evidence base is a single seed round on
single prints of each design ($n = 1$ article per geometry, with one
triplicate); the drop protocol probes one height, one impact surface,
and axial loading only; the specimens never leave the elastic regime,
so crush-energy metrics await the quasi-static campaign; per-specimen
energy absorption in joules is not recoverable from the current rig
(the falling-mass and displacement channels required for a force
integral are not instrumented); one tested article lacks a design
mapping and one seed design's official article assignment carries a
recorded discrepancy; and all results are from a single printer,
material pair, and cell topology. The metal-analog protocol
(Section~\ref{sec:methods:validation}) and the pre-registered
revision plan above are the designed responses to these limits.
```

---

## `\section{Conclusions}` — lines 1415–1439

**Lines 1420–1439** (full Conclusions text):
```
We have presented an experiment-driven Bayesian-optimization framework
for designing multi-material 3D-printed tensegrity-inspired energy
absorbers using PLA struts and TPU tension elements, and we have
closed its first loop on physical hardware. The framework
parameterizes a five-variable $T_3$-prism family under a constant-mass
fairness projection, fabricates each candidate in a single
multi-material FDM build with TPU tendons anchored inside the PLA
strut ends, characterizes every article with 101 instrumented drops,
and updates a fully Bayesian Gaussian-process
surrogate~\citep{balandat2020botorch, eriksson2021saasbo} that
recommends the next batch. In the nine-design seed round the filtered
peak-acceleration ratio spanned 0.89 to 1.06 against sub-percent
repeatability, one design crossed into genuine attenuation, and the
first model-recommended batch of nine designs has been generated and
sent to fabrication. \todo{Add the round-2 headline (predicted versus
measured, hypervolume gain over the budget-matched baseline) once the
batch is tested.} The approach is broadly applicable to architected
absorbers whose constitutive response is difficult to calibrate from
first principles and where physical experiments, rather than
simulations, are the natural ground truth.
```

## manuscript.pdf — Full Inspection Report

---

### 1. Title

**Bayesian Optimization of Multi-Material 3D-Printed Tensegrity-Inspired Structures for Energy Absorption**

(Rendered across the top of page 1 in a two-column ASME-journal layout, split across lines xxiii–xxvi.)

---

### 2. Abstract — Text (verbatim from PDF / .tex, identical)

> Tensegrity-inspired architectures combine rigid compression members with a network of soft tension elements, yielding lightweight assemblies with tunable nonlinear responses that are attractive for impact mitigation in aerospace landing structures and related protective applications. Multi-material fused-deposition modeling (FDM) of polylactic acid (PLA) struts and thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) tension elements makes it possible to fabricate pre-assembled tensegrity-inspired geometries rapidly enough to support an experiment-driven design search. We report a closed-loop Bayesian optimization (BO) framework in which a fully Bayesian Gaussian-process surrogate is trained directly on instrumented drop-tower measurements and used to recommend the next batch of designs to print and test. A three-strut prism family is parameterized by five continuous geometry variables under a constant-mass fairness constraint, and each printed specimen is characterized by more than one hundred repeated drops. The campaign minimizes two impact objectives: the filtered peak-acceleration ratio across the specimen and a mass-weighted score for the rebound motion returned to the payload. We report the nine-specimen quasi-random seed round, the resulting surrogate diagnostics and Pareto set, and the first model-recommended batch, and we describe a metal-analog validation protocol that tests whether learned design rankings transfer across material systems.

---

# Campaign-Count Consistency Audit — `manuscript-body.tex`

Below are **exact passages with line numbers** for every requested topic, followed by a contradiction inventory. No editorial judgment is made; contradictions are stated as factual mismatches between passages.

---

## 1. Seed Designs / Specimens / Articles

| Location | Line(s) | Exact text |
|---|---|---|
| Abstract | 158–159 | "We report the **nine-specimen quasi-random seed round**…" |
| Intro status TODO | 184–186 | "the **nine-specimen Sobol seed batch** plus the reference prism have been printed and drop-tested (101 drops per specimen)" |
| Methods – Budget/seeding | 1007–1009 | "The seed round is an **n = 9 Sobol draw** with a recorded seed over the five-variable box, printed together with the fixed reference prism (S0)." |
| Methods – Table caption | 577–580 | "The seed round is an **n=9 Sobol draw** (fixed seed) over this box, with each design then projected onto the constant solid-mass budget m⋆=30.95 g." |
| Results – Seed-Round | 1140–1143 | "**All nine Sobol specimens and the reference prism** were printed and declared acceptable to test; **eight articles** (six mapped Sobol designs, the reference prism, and one article pending a design mapping) have completed 101-drop characterization sessions to date…" |
| Results – Table caption | 1176–1192 | Table lists **8 rows**: Spec 01, (unmapped), Spec 05, S0 ref., Spec 00, Spec 04, Spec 02, Spec 08. Footer note: "Spec 03 was tested but its session was not yet uploaded at the time of writing; specs 06 and 07 are printed and pending test." |
| Conclusions | 1430–1431 | "In the **nine-design seed round** the filtered peak-acceleration ratio spanned 0.89 to 1.06…" |

**Contradiction A — "nine specimens" vs. "eight articles" tested:**
- Abstract (L158–159), Intro TODO (L184–186), Methods (L1007–1009), and Conclusions (L1430) all say "nine-specimen seed round."
- Results (L1140–1143) states only **eight articles** have completed 101-drop sessions; the table (L1176–1192) lists eight rows; the caption notes Spec 03 session not yet uploaded and Specs 06 & 07 pending test. So at the time of writing, **three of the nine Sobol specimens have not been fully characterized**, yet the abstract and conclusions describe the seed round as complete.

---

## 2. Tested / Mapped Articles

| Location | Line(s) | Exact text |
|---|---|---|
| Results – Seed-Round | 1140–1143 | "eight articles (**six mapped Sobol designs**, the reference prism, and **one article pending a design mapping**) have completed 101-drop characterization sessions" |
| Results – Pareto | 1217–1219 | "Pareto membership is evaluated over the **seven articles with both objectives**; amdjwm is omitted because its missing weighed mass prevents computing E_reb." |
| Results – Surrogate audit | 1258–1260 | "leave-one-out predictions for t_180 had a mean absolute percentage error of 2.6% and Pearson r = 0.70 across **seven articles**" |
| Methods – BO mass treatment | 933–935 | "The seed data show an apparent trade-off driven substantially by the single strongest attenuator; at **seven mapped articles** it is not statistically resolved (Spearman ρ = −0.39, p = 0.38)" |
| Discussion | 1334–1335 | "the apparent t_180-versus-rebound trade-off is driven substantially by the single strongest attenuator (Spearman ρ = −0.39, p = 0.38 across **the reliable articles**)" |
| Results – Seed-Round | 1158–1160 | "printed mass correlates strongly with t_180 (r = 0.83, p = 0.02, **n = 7**)" |
| Discussion – Mass confound | 1349–1351 | "printed mass correlates with t_180 at r = 0.83" (no n stated) |

**Contradiction B — "eight articles completed" vs. surrogate/Pareto fit on "seven":**
- L1140–1143 says eight articles completed 101-drop sessions.
- L1217–1219, L1258–1260, L933–935, and L1158–1160 all use **n = 7** for the surrogate fit and Pareto evaluation, because amdjwm (the unmapped article) lacks a weighed mass and is excluded. The text never explicitly reconciles why eight completed sessions yield only seven usable data points for both objectives simultaneously; the exclusion reason (missing mass → no E_reb) is stated only in the table footnote (L1188–1190) and the Pareto paragraph (L1218–1219).

---

## 3. Reference Prism Treatment

| Location | Line(s) | Exact text |
|---|---|---|
| Intro status TODO | 184–186 | "the nine-specimen Sobol seed batch **plus the reference prism** have been printed and drop-tested" |
| Methods – Budget/seeding | 1007–1009 | "printed together with the **fixed reference prism (S0)**" |
| Methods – Constant-mass | 556–558 | "its solid CAD mass … equals m⋆ = 30.95 g, **the solid mass of the reference prism**" |
| Results – Table | 1203 | "S0 ref. \| bpx68c \| 20.23 \| 1.0111 ± 0.0024 \| 6.2 \| 468" |
| Results – Pareto | 1220–1221 | "The observed Pareto set comprises three articles (**6lhxfy, 6nheas, and the reference prism bpx68c**)." |

No internal contradiction found for the reference prism. It is consistently described as S0, printed alongside the nine Sobol specimens, and used as the mass-budget anchor (m⋆ = 30.95 g solid mass). Its as-printed mass (20.23 g, L1203) is lower than the solid-mass budget, consistent with the partial-infill discussion.

---

## 4. 101 Drops

| Location | Line(s) | Exact text |
|---|---|---|
| Abstract | 153–154 | "each printed specimen is characterized by **more than one hundred repeated drops**" |
| Intro Contribution 2 | 270–272 | "**101 repeated instrumented drops per specimen**, standardized SAE J211 filtering" |
| Methods – Drop-tower | 785–786 | "a full **101-drop specimen characterization** completes in about ninety minutes" |
| Methods – Per-specimen objectives | 806–808 | "Each drop session contributes **101 valid captures** to the stabilized statistics (**103 for one article, autv5r**), counted after the first two drops of each session are discarded as warm-up." |
| Results – Table caption | 1178–1180 | "**101 valid captures per article (103 for autv5r)** at 60 in onto the standardized polyurethane surface … counted after the first two warm-up drops of each session were discarded." |
| Conclusions | 1427–1428 | "characterizes every article with **101 instrumented drops**" |

**Contradiction C — "101 drops" vs. "103 for autv5r":**
- Abstract (L153–154) says "more than one hundred repeated drops" (consistent with both 101 and 103).
- Intro Contribution 2 (L270–272) and Conclusions (L1427–1428) state flatly "101 repeated instrumented drops per specimen" with no qualification for the 103-drop exception.
- Methods (L806–808) and the Results table caption (L1178–1180) correctly note the 103-drop exception for autv5r.
- The Conclusions (L1427–1428) say "101 instrumented drops" without acknowledging the 103-drop case.

---

## 5. Round-2 Designs (Recommended Batch)

| Location | Line(s) | Exact text |
|---|---|---|
| Intro status TODO | 187–190 | "the first model-recommended batch of **nine designs** is on the printer. Section 5 reports the seed round; **round-2 outcomes** … remain placeholders pending data." |
| Methods – Budget/seeding | 1010–1012 | "Optimization proceeds in sequential batches of **q = 9 prints** … the first model-recommended batch (**Ax trials 10 to 18**) is reported in Section 5." |
| Results – Pareto | 1221–1224 | "The **nine recommended designs** (Ax trials 10 to 18) concentrate in the low-t_180 region…; they have been sliced and sent to the printer…" |
| Results – Later-Round Placeholders | 1293–1296 | "**Round-2 outcomes**, the budget-matched baseline comparison, the SAASBO-versus-standard-GP calibration audit, and the replicate-article repeatability study are **pending data**…" |
| Conclusions | 1432–1434 | "the first model-recommended batch of **nine designs** has been generated and sent to fabrication." |
| Abstract TODO | 162–163 | "Tighten abstract toward 150–200 words with concrete **round-2 numerical results** once the next batch is tested." |

No numerical contradiction in round-2 counts: all passages agree on **nine designs, Ax trials 10–18**. However, Methods (L1010–1012) says the batch "is reported in Section 5," while Results (L1293–1296) explicitly states round-2 outcomes are **pending data** — a forward-reference inconsistency (the Methods section promises results that the Results section defers).

---

## 6. Objective Names

| Location | Line(s) | Exact text |
|---|---|---|
| Abstract | 155–157 | "two impact objectives: the **filtered peak-acceleration ratio** across the specimen and a **mass-weighted score for the rebound motion** returned to the payload" |
| Intro Contribution 2 | 272–275 | "two per-specimen objectives (**the filtered peak-acceleration ratio across the specimen** and a **mass-weighted rebound score**)" |
| Methods – BO loop | 927–932 | "simultaneously minimize the **filtered peak-acceleration ratio t_180** and the **per-drop rebound score E_reb**" |
| Eq. (1) label | 822–824 | "t_180 is the CFC-180 **filtered peak-acceleration ratio** … E_reb is a **provisional mass-weighted rebound score** with units of energy (millijoules per drop)" |
| Table 3 caption | 1183–1185 | "E_reb uses each article's weighed mass per Eq. (1). The ringdown frequency f_n is a **print-health descriptor, not an objective**." |
| Novelty table | 397 | "Experiment-driven BO (**SAASBO/qNEHVI**)" |

**Contradiction D — "provisional" qualifier dropped in Conclusions:**
- Methods (L822–824) explicitly calls E_reb a "**provisional** mass-weighted rebound score."
- Abstract (L155–157) and Conclusions (L1424–1428) describe the two objectives without the "provisional" qualifier, presenting E_reb as a settled objective.
- Discussion (L1329–1344) and Methods (L848–850) state the rebound score "is slated to become a **constraint** once validated," meaning it may not remain an objective at all — yet the abstract and conclusions frame it as a campaign objective without caveat.

---

## 7. Constant-Mass Claim

| Location | Line(s) | Exact text |
|---|---|---|
| Abstract | 152–154 | "parameterized by five continuous geometry variables under a **constant-mass fairness constraint**" |
| Intro Contribution 1 | 266–268 | "Candidate designs are compared fairly through a **constant-mass projection** that rescales every geometry to a common material budget before printing" |
| Methods – Constant-mass | 549–558 | "Every candidate is therefore projected onto a **constant material budget** before printing … until its solid CAD mass … equals m⋆ = 30.95 g … converged to within 0.15 g on rendered geometry." |
| Methods – Limitation | 565–570 | "The choice of a **solid-mass budget has a documented limitation** … PLA struts print at partial infill while thin TPU cables print near solid, so **as-printed masses still ranged from 18.50 to 22.29 g** across the seed batch" |
| Discussion – Mass confound | 1347–1351 | "Holding **solid CAD mass constant did not hold printed grams constant**: PLA prints at partial infill while thin TPU cables print near solid, so the seed articles span 18.50–22.29 g and printed mass correlates with t_180 at r = 0.83." |
| Conclusions | 1424–1425 | "parameterizes a five-variable T_3-prism family under a **constant-mass fairness projection**" |

**Contradiction E — "constant-mass constraint" vs. 18.50–22.29 g spread:**
- Abstract (L152–154) and Conclusions (L1424–1425) describe the constant-mass projection as a "fairness constraint" without qualification.
- Methods (L565–570) and Discussion (L1347–1351) explicitly state the constraint **failed to hold printed grams constant**, with a 3.79 g spread (18.50–22.29 g) and r = 0.83 correlation of printed mass with the primary objective. The abstract and conclusions do not disclose this failure.

---

## 8. SAASBO / qNEHVI

| Location | Line(s) | Exact text |
|---|---|---|
| Intro Contribution 3 | 278–281 | "An experiment-driven BO loop, built on BoTorch/Ax … with a **fully Bayesian sparse-prior surrogate (SAASBO)** … that ingests the physical drop measurements … and recommends the next batch" |
